title: A martyrdom in line with the gospel
sum: The church of Smyrna writes to the church of Philomelium and to churches everywhere about the martyrs of a recent persecution, and above all about Polycarp, whose death 'set a seal' on it and ended it (1:0-1). Almost everything, the writers say, happened so that the Lord might show 'a martyrdom in line with the gospel': Polycarp waited to be handed over, as the Lord did, so that we may imitate him and care for others as well as ourselves (1:2).
The opening states the purpose of the whole letter. It is not only a report; it is a lesson in how a Christian should face death.

views.H: Lake calls the letter 'obviously genuine and contemporary', 'the earliest known history of a Christian martyrdom, the genuineness of which is unquestionable'. Bart Ehrman argues that it was written decades later by someone who claimed to be an eyewitness (the note at 1:1).
views.N: The phrase 'in line with the gospel' (1:1; 19:1; 22:1) is the key: the writer will point out each likeness to Jesus' passion. Lake's margin adds Jude 2 (the greeting) and Philippians 2:4 (1:2).
views.M: The martyr is an imitator of the Lord (1:2; 17:3) and a model for others to imitate (19:1). Throughout the letter the language of witness means dying for Christ (the note at 1:1).
views.R: The letter goes from one city of the province of Asia to another, Philomelium, and Philomelium is to send it on 'to the brothers farther away' (20:1).

settings.what: The letter of the church of Smyrna about Polycarp's martyrdom: greeting and purpose
settings.by: The church of Smyrna (the writer named in 20:1 is Marcion, or Marcus or Marcianus; the scribe was Evarestus, 20:2)
settings.to: The church at Philomelium and 'all the communities of the holy and catholic church in every place' (1:0)
settings.when: Lake: a 'contemporary' account, written soon after the death; Bart Ehrman: decades later (the note at 1:1). On the year of the death (155, 156 or later) see 21:1.
settings.why: To give the full story of the martyrs, so that the readers may glorify God (20:1) and learn to imitate a death 'in line with the gospel'. Knowing that it was written for churches who might face the same trials changes its tone: it is a model to follow, not only news.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: No longer human beings but angels
sum: All martyrdoms that come by the will of God are blessed and noble (2:1). The writers tell of Christians torn by whips until their veins and arteries showed, who endured without a groan, so that the Lord seemed to be standing beside them (2:2); who bought eternal life with one hour of pain, found the fire cold, and looked to the good things 'no ear has heard and no eye has seen' (2:3); and who were laid on trumpet shells and tortured to make them deny (2:4).

views.H: Eusebius gives these chapters only in his own summary (Church History 4.15.4). The Moscow manuscript and the others differ at 2:3 between 'eternal life' and 'eternal punishment' (variant).
views.N: 1 Corinthians 2:9 (Lake's margin), 2 Corinthians 5:8, 2 Timothy 4:17 and Daniel 3 stand behind the account. The martyrs are 'already angels' (2:3), a figure that goes beyond Matthew 22:30.
views.M: The martyrs' calm is a sign of the Lord's presence. The account praises endurance without praising pain: it is 'by the will of God' (2:1), not chosen.
views.R: The letter says the tortures were meant to turn the martyrs to denial (2:4), and it calls the judge who ordered them 'the tyrant'.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 2:9; Isaiah 64:4; 2 Corinthians 5:8; 2 Timothy 4:17; Acts 7:55-56; Daniel 3:25-27; Matthew 22:30; Hebrews 11:35-37

settings.by: The church of Smyrna (the writer named in 20:1 is Marcion, or Marcus or Marcianus; the scribe was Evarestus, 20:2)
settings.to: The church at Philomelium and 'all the communities of the holy and catholic church in every place' (1:0)
settings.when: Before Polycarp's arrest, in the same persecution
settings.why: To praise those who endured, and to show that their courage came from God.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: Germanicus
sum: The devil did not win against them all. Young Germanicus, urged by the proconsul to pity his own youth, pulled the beast onto himself (3:1). His courage made the crowd shout: 'Away with the atheists! Let Polycarp be searched for!' (3:2).

views.H: Eusebius tells Germanicus's story in summary (Church History 4.15.5-6).
views.M: Germanicus is the model of the right kind of courage: he did not give himself up, but once condemned he faced death without flinching (contrast Quintus, 4:1).
views.R: To the crowd, Christians were 'atheists', people who denied the gods of the city and of Rome. The cry turns against the city's best-known Christian, Polycarp.

settings.by: The crowd in the stadium at Smyrna
settings.to: The proconsul and the city
settings.when: After Germanicus's death in the arena
settings.why: To show how Polycarp came to be sought: the letter puts the crowd's cry right after its amazement at the nobility of the Christians (3:2).
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: The man who gave himself up
sum: Quintus, a newcomer from Phrygia, had urged himself and others to come forward of their own accord. When he saw the beasts he lost his nerve, and the proconsul persuaded him to swear and sacrifice. 'That is why, brothers, we give no praise to people who turn themselves in, because that is not what the gospel teaches' (4:1).

views.H: Eusebius draws the same lesson in his own words (Church History 4.15.7-8). The letter says nothing more about Quintus's background.
views.N: Lake's margin gives Matthew 10:23, 'escape to the next' town, as the gospel teaching meant.
views.M: The church's rule: do not seek martyrdom, do not deny Christ when it comes. The Catholic Encyclopedia cites Gregory of Nazianzus: 'it is mere rashness to seek death, but it is cowardly to refuse it'.

settings.by: The church of Smyrna (the writer named in 20:1 is Marcion, or Marcus or Marcianus; the scribe was Evarestus, 20:2)
settings.to: The church at Philomelium and 'all the communities of the holy and catholic church in every place' (1:0)
settings.when: After the story of Quintus
settings.why: To warn the churches, in a time of persecution, against reckless zeal that ends in denial.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: The burning pillow
sum: Polycarp was not upset when he heard and wanted to stay in the city, but his friends urged him to leave, and he went to a small farm, praying night and day for everyone and for the churches of the world (5:1). Three days before his arrest he saw his pillow burning and told those with him, 'I must be burned alive' (5:2).

views.N: His withdrawal fits Matthew 10:23; his prayer for the churches recalls John 17.
views.M: Polycarp neither runs from death in fear nor rushes to it: he waits, prays and accepts God's sign.
views.H: The vision is presented as a true prophecy, fulfilled in 12:3. Eusebius gives it in summary (Church History 4.15.10).

settings.by: The church of Smyrna (the writer named in 20:1 is Marcion, or Marcus or Marcianus; the scribe was Evarestus, 20:2)
settings.to: The church at Philomelium and 'all the communities of the holy and catholic church in every place' (1:0)
settings.when: In the days before his arrest
settings.why: To show Polycarp's calm and his obedience: he leaves at his friends' request and learns from God how he will die.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

settings.what: Polycarp's saying after the vision: 'I must be burned alive'
settings.by: Polycarp
settings.to: the few friends with him on the farm
settings.when: three days before his arrest
settings.why: To tell them what the vision meant, and to prepare them for his death
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: Betrayed by his own household
sum: The searchers came to the second farm, seized two slave boys, and tortured one until he told where Polycarp was (6:1). It was impossible for him to stay hidden, for his betrayers were of his own household, and the police captain, named Herod, was eager to bring him into the stadium, so that Polycarp might share Christ's lot and his betrayers Judas's punishment (6:2).

views.N: Lake's margin: Matthew 10:36. The names Herod and Judas are the writer's clearest pointers to the passion.
views.H: Lake: 'The writer desires to bring out the points of resemblance to the Passion of Christ. The coincidences are remarkable, but none are in themselves at all improbable.'
views.R: A local official, the eirēnarchos, makes the arrest; the proconsul will judge.

settings.by: The church of Smyrna (the writer named in 20:1 is Marcion, or Marcus or Marcianus; the scribe was Evarestus, 20:2)
settings.to: The church at Philomelium and 'all the communities of the holy and catholic church in every place' (1:0)
settings.when: Polycarp at the second farm
settings.why: To show that his capture was not his choice and that it matched the Lord's.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: May God's will be done
sum: On Friday evening police and horsemen came out as if against a bandit and found him in an upstairs room. He could have escaped but would not: 'May God's will be done' (7:1). He came down, talked with them, had food and drink set before them, and asked for an hour to pray (7:2). He prayed aloud for two hours, and many were sorry they had come against so godly an old man (7:3).

views.N: Matthew 26:55 (as against a bandit), Acts 21:14 and Matthew 6:10 (God's will), and Gethsemane's hour of prayer (Matthew 26:40).
views.M: The arrest scene shows the martyr's freedom: he could flee and does not; he feeds his captors; he prays. Eusebius keeps the scene in summary (Church History 4.15.11-14).
views.H: The Moscow manuscript and the others add 'in a small room' to Eusebius's 'in an upper room' (variant).

settings.what: Polycarp's prayer before his arrest, reported
settings.by: Polycarp
settings.to: God, in the hearing of those who came to arrest him
settings.when: With the arresting party waiting below
settings.why: The letter does not give the words, only that he remembered 'everyone who had ever come his way' and 'the whole catholic church throughout the world'. It shows the shepherd praying for his flock to the last.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: Lord Caesar
sum: After his prayer they set him on a donkey and brought him into the city on 'a great Sabbath' (8:1). Herod and his father Nicetes took him into their carriage and urged him: 'What harm is there in saying "Lord Caesar," and offering sacrifice?' He said, 'I am not going to do what you are urging me to do' (8:2). They took him down from the carriage in such a hurry that he scraped his shin, and he walked on into the roaring stadium (8:3).

views.N: The donkey (John 12:14), the 'great Sabbath' (John 19:31) and a Herod (Luke 23) frame the scene.
views.R: The test was a few words and a sacrifice: say 'Lord Caesar' and sacrifice, 'and so save yourself' (8:2). Lake and Eusebius read the words as a title; whether they were also heard as a confession set against 'Jesus is Lord' (1 Corinthians 12:3), the text leaves open (the note at 8:2). Tertullian later wrote that he would call the emperor 'Lord' only 'in the common acceptation of the word' (Apology 34). The carriage (Latin carruca, Lake) shows Herod and Nicetes as men of rank.
views.H: The 'great Sabbath' is one of the clues to the date: Lake reports Turner's and Schwartz's arguments that it fixes 22 February 156 (see chapter 21).

settings.what: Herod and Nicetes try to persuade Polycarp
settings.by: Herod the police captain and his father Nicetes
settings.to: Polycarp, in their carriage
settings.when: on the way into Smyrna, before the trial
settings.why: To persuade him to say the words and sacrifice, 'and so save yourself' (8:2), in private before the trial. His refusal comes before his two answers in the stadium (9:3; 10:1).
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: Eighty-six years
sum: As he entered the stadium, a voice came from heaven: 'Be strong, Polycarp, and show courage' (9:1). The proconsul urged him: 'Respect your age. Swear by the fortune of Caesar. Repent. Say, "Away with the atheists!"' Polycarp looked at the crowd, waved his hand at them, and said, 'Away with the atheists!' (9:2). Pressed to curse Christ, he answered: 'For eighty-six years I have been his slave, and he has never wronged me. How can I speak evil of my King, the one who saved me?' (9:3).

views.N: The voice's words are Joshua 1:6 in Greek; 'my King' sets Christ against Caesar.
views.M: The most quoted words of any martyr act. Polycarp turns each demand around: he says 'Away with the atheists' of the pagans, and he refuses to insult the King he has served all his life.
views.R: The oath 'by the fortune of Caesar' was the usual test; Lake notes that the Latin oath was 'per genium' or 'sometimes fortunam', hence the Greek tychē, and that Christians refused it but would swear 'by the safety of Caesar' (Tertullian, Apology 32). The proconsul's 'Respect your age' is a plea to an old man.
views.H: Lake takes 'eighty-six years' most likely as Polycarp's whole life: 'probably a Christian born, unless we ascribe to him a quite improbable age'. Bart Ehrman finds the scene impossible as history: animal hunts in a 'stadium' rather than an amphitheater, and 'only a summary mock trial that does not follow any known legal precedent' (deep section).

deep.b:
Chapters 9-11 are a trial in three rounds. The proconsul offers release three times on the same terms: deny, swear by Caesar's fortune, curse Christ, repent (9:2-3; 10:1; 11:1-2). Polycarp answers three times: 'Away with the atheists' (9:2), 'Eighty-six years' (9:3), and 'I am a Christian' (10:1). Then come threats of beasts and fire, and Polycarp's answer that the proconsul's fire lasts an hour (11:2). The herald's announcement, 'Polycarp has confessed that he is a Christian' (12:1), is the only verdict given.

Eusebius quotes the whole trial (Church History 4.15.17-25). Lake judges the account 'obviously genuine and contemporary'. Bart Ehrman judges the scene not a real trial: 'there is no official trial of the condemned, but only a summary mock trial that does not follow any known legal precedent', and the beast-fights could not have been held in a 'stadium', which 'would most properly denote a race track', rather than an amphitheater (his blog, 2023, from Forgery and Counterforgery, 2013). Lake does not take up these points. The text itself shows a proconsul giving way to the crowd at public games (12:2-3); Claude's theory on the book page reads the scene that way.

The proconsul demands an oath by Caesar's tychē, 'fortune'. Lake's footnote: the customary oath was 'per genium (or sometimes fortunam, hence τύχην) Caesaris', by the emperor's genius or fortune, which Christians 'rejected', while they accepted the oath 'per salutem Caesaris', 'by the safety of Caesar'. Tertullian explains why: the genii are demons, and 'we have been in the habit of exorcising them, not of swearing by them' (Apology 32, ANF). Whether Christians may swear oaths at all, a different question, is on the site's cards at Matthew 5 and in the Histories of Tacitus 4.

echoes: Joshua 1:6; 1 Corinthians 16:13; John 12:28; John 19:15; Matthew 5:33-37; Acts 26:28

settings.by: a voice from heaven (the speaker unseen)
settings.to: Polycarp, heard by the Christians present
settings.when: as he entered the stadium
settings.why: To strengthen him for the trial, as God strengthened Joshua.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

settings.what: The trial: the proconsul and Polycarp
settings.by: the proconsul Statius Quadratus (21:1) and Polycarp
settings.to: each other, before the crowd in the stadium
settings.when: on the day of the great Sabbath (8:1), after the animal hunts had been closed (12:2)
settings.why: For the proconsul, to get the old man to deny Christ and avoid an execution; for Polycarp, to confess Christ plainly and give honor to the ruler without denying his King.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: I am a Christian
sum: Asked again to swear by Caesar's fortune, Polycarp says: 'If you vainly imagine that I will swear ... listen plainly: I am a Christian. And if you want to learn what Christianity teaches, set a day and hear me' (10:1). Told to persuade the people, he answers that Christians are taught to honor rulers appointed by God, as long as it does them no harm, but the mob does not deserve a defense (10:2).

views.N: Romans 13:1 and 1 Peter 2:13 (Lake's margin): rulers are appointed by God, and Christians give them honor.
views.R: Polycarp's answer draws the line between honor and worship: he will reason with the governor as a lawful ruler, but he will not swear by the emperor's spirit or plead before a crowd.
views.M: 'I am a Christian' becomes the classic confession of the martyrs: the name alone is the charge.

title: A fire that burns for an hour
sum: 'I have wild beasts,' the proconsul says. 'Call them,' Polycarp answers: a change from better to worse is no repentance for us (11:1). Threatened with fire, he says: 'You threaten a fire that burns for an hour and is soon put out. For you do not know the fire of the coming judgment ... Bring on whatever you want' (11:2).

views.N: The eternal fire of Matthew 25:41 and Mark 9:48.
views.M: The martyr's freedom from fear rests on the judgment to come: a short fire is nothing beside the fire that does not end (compare 2:3).

title: The teacher of Asia
sum: Full of courage, joy and grace, Polycarp unsettles the proconsul, who has his herald proclaim three times: 'Polycarp has confessed that he is a Christian' (12:1). The crowd of Gentiles and Jews shouts that he is 'the teacher of Asia, the father of the Christians, the destroyer of our gods', and asks Philip the Asiarch for a lion, but the games are over (12:2). So they shout for fire, and the vision of the pillow comes true (12:3).

views.R: The Asiarch, a priest of the emperor's cult in the province (LSJ), says he has closed the animal hunts. The crowd's charge, that Polycarp taught people 'not to sacrifice or to worship', is the heart of the pagan case against Christians.
views.H: The letter names 'Jews' in the crowd here and in 13:1, 17:2 and 18:1, which Eusebius keeps (see the note at 12:2).
views.N: The face full of grace recalls Stephen (Acts 6:15). Revelation had warned Smyrna's church of 'the slander that comes from those who say they are Jews and are not' (Revelation 2:9).

settings.by: the proconsul's herald
settings.to: the crowd in the stadium
settings.when: after the trial
settings.why: To announce the offense: confessing the name. It serves as a sentence.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

settings.by: the crowd of Gentiles and Jews living in Smyrna
settings.to: the proconsul and the Asiarch Philip
settings.when: after the herald's announcement
settings.why: To demand Polycarp's death, first by a lion, then by fire.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: The pyre
sum: The crowds quickly gathered wood from workshops and baths, the Jews eagerly helping (13:1). Polycarp took off his clothes and tried to take off his sandals, which the faithful had always done for him, eager to touch him (13:2). When they were about to nail him, he said, 'Leave me as I am', for God would let him stay on the pyre without the nails (13:3).

views.M: The honor the faithful gave Polycarp in life, each eager to be first to touch his skin (13:2), comes before the honor they give his body and bones (17:1; 18:2).
views.H: Eusebius quotes the chapter (Church History 4.15.29-31), including the line about the Jews (see the note at 13:1); at 13:2 his copy says Polycarp was honored 'even before his gray hair', where the manuscripts say 'before his martyrdom' (variant).

settings.what: Polycarp's words to the men about to nail him
settings.by: Polycarp
settings.to: the men preparing the pyre
settings.when: at the pyre, before he was tied
settings.why: To ask to be left unnailed, trusting that God, who lets him endure the fire, will keep him still on the pyre.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: The prayer at the stake
sum: Tied to the stake, 'like a choice ram ... a whole burnt offering', Polycarp looks up to heaven and prays (14:1). He blesses God for counting him worthy to share 'in the cup of your Christ' for the resurrection of soul and body, and asks to be taken in 'as a sacrifice rich and acceptable' (14:2). He ends with praise through 'the eternal and heavenly high priest Jesus Christ, your beloved servant', with glory to the Father 'with him and the Holy Spirit' (14:3; Eusebius's copy: 'with him, in the Holy Spirit').

views.N: Genesis 22:13 (the ram), Mark 10:38-39 (the cup), John 5:29 (Lake's margin: the resurrection to life), Titus 1:2 (the God who does not lie), Hebrews 4:14 (the high priest).
views.M: The prayer turns death into worship: the martyr offers himself as a sacrifice, as Paul spoke of being 'poured out as a drink offering' (Philippians 2:17).

deep.b: The prayer has three parts. Address: God Almighty, Father of 'your beloved and blessed servant Jesus Christ', God of angels, of creation and of the righteous (14:1). Thanksgiving: for 'this day and this hour', a share 'in the cup of your Christ', resurrection 'of soul and body' (14:2). Doxology: 'through the eternal and heavenly high priest Jesus Christ ... through him be glory to you, with him and the Holy Spirit' (14:3). Eusebius quotes it in full (Church History 4.15.32-35), and his Greek differs in three places that matter: no address 'Lord God, the Almighty' (14:1), no 'heavenly', and 'with him, in the Holy Spirit' (14:3); see the variants. His Greek has the same word pais for Jesus; the NPNF English renders it 'Son'.

echoes: Genesis 22:13; Leviticus 1:9; Revelation 4:8; Mark 10:38-39; John 5:29; 1 Corinthians 15:42; Titus 1:2; Hebrews 4:14; Philippians 2:17

settings.by: Polycarp
settings.to: God the Father, in the hearing of the crowd and of the Christians present
settings.when: bound to the stake, before the fire was lit
settings.why: To give thanks for his death as a share in Christ's cup and to offer himself as a sacrifice. For the letter's readers it was a model of how to pray at the hour of death.
settings.readers: The church at Philomelium, which had asked Smyrna for a full account (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which it was to send the letter on (20:1); and the Christians of Smyrna themselves, who would gather each year at Polycarp's grave on the day of his death (18:3).

title: A vault of fire
sum: When the fire was lit, the Christians who were there saw a wonder (15:1): the flames formed a vault, like a ship's sail filled with wind, around the body, which was not like burning flesh but like bread baking or gold refined in a furnace, and gave off a scent like incense (15:2). Eusebius's copy has no bread, only the gold and silver (variant).

views.N: Daniel 3 (the furnace), Zechariah 13:9 and 1 Peter 1:7 (gold refined), 2 Corinthians 2:15 and Leviticus 1:9 (the sweet smell).
views.M: The martyr's body becomes an offering pleasing to God; the fire that should destroy it honors it.
views.H: The writers claim to be eyewitnesses (15:1). Eusebius quotes the passage (Church History 4.15.36-37) without the loaf of 15:2 (variant). The text claims a wonder; it is among the miracles of the account that readers weigh differently (see the book's reliability section).

deep.title: Claude's theory: a martyrdom shaped like the Lord's Supper
deep.b:
This is Claude's own reading, offered as a theory. Chapters 14-15 gather words that belong to the church's meal: Polycarp gives thanks (eulogō, 'I bless'), speaks of 'the cup of your Christ', offers himself 'as a sacrifice rich and acceptable', and in the fire becomes 'like a loaf in the oven'. Ignatius, whom Polycarp knew, had written that he wanted to be 'God's wheat ... ground, that I may be found pure bread' (quoted in Eusebius, Church History 3.36.12). If the writers had Ignatius's image and the meal in mind, they were presenting the martyr's death as a living Eucharist: thanksgiving, cup, bread and offering.

Against it: the loaf is not in Eusebius's copy of the letter (variant), so the theory rests on the wording of the Greek manuscripts Lake prints. The text never names the Lord's Supper, and the 'cup' has a plain Gospel meaning of suffering (Mark 10:38). This remains a possible reading, not a proven one.

echoes: Daniel 3:25-27; Zechariah 13:9; 1 Peter 1:7; Malachi 3:3; 2 Corinthians 2:15; Leviticus 1:9; Ephesians 5:2

title: The dove and the dagger
sum: Since the fire would not consume him, the executioner was ordered to stab him with a dagger; a dove came out, and so much blood that it put out the fire, and the crowd marveled at the difference between unbelievers and the chosen (16:1). Polycarp was one of those chosen: 'an apostolic and prophetic teacher, overseer of the catholic church in Smyrna', whose every word has been fulfilled (16:2).

views.H: Three readings of the Greek matter here: the dove (missing in Eusebius; emended away by Wordsworth), the dagger (Eusebius: 'sword'), and 'catholic' (with Eusebius) or 'holy' (with the Moscow manuscript and the Latin). All are set out in the variant entries.
views.N: The dove recalls the Spirit at Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:16); the blood recalls John 19:34.
views.M: Polycarp's title, 'overseer of the catholic church in Smyrna', is the first time in the letter he is called overseer. The title Lake prints above the letter calls him 'overseer of Smyrna', though each manuscript has its own title (the note at 1:0).

title: We worship him; we love the martyrs
sum: The devil, seeing Polycarp crowned with the crown of incorruption, made sure the Christians could not take his body (17:1). At the Jews' urging, Nicetes asked the governor not to give it up, 'or else they will abandon the crucified one and start to worship this man'. They did not know, the writers say, that 'we will never be able to abandon Christ ... or to worship anyone else' (17:2). 'For Christ we worship, because he is the Son of God. The martyrs we love as disciples and imitators of the Lord' (17:3).

views.M: The letter states the difference between the worship given to Christ (proskynoumen) and the love given to the martyrs (agapōmen). The churches differ on what honors that love allows (see the deep section).
views.R: The officials feared a new cult at a tomb. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Roman officials 'usually permitted relatives or friends to gather up the mutilated remains of the martyrs for interment, although in some instances such permission was refused'; here, the letter says, Nicetes asked the governor not to give up the body (17:2).
views.H: Eusebius quotes the chapter in full (Church History 4.15.40-42); in his copy 'certain people', not the evil one, prompt Nicetes, and the words 'the blameless one for sinners' are missing (variants). The role given to 'the Jews' is discussed at 12:2.

deep.b:
The letter answers a charge: that Christians would worship Polycarp instead of Christ. Its answer has two verbs. Christ we worship (proskynoumen) 'because he is the Son of God'; the martyrs we love (agapōmen) 'as disciples and imitators of the Lord'. The officials' fear uses a third verb, sebesthai, 'to worship, honour' (17:2). Proskyneō itself had a wide range: LSJ gives 'fall down and worship' of the gods and also 'prostrating oneself before kings and superiors'. The letter keeps it for Christ and gives the martyrs love.

Later the churches drew the line in other words. The Catholic Encyclopedia's article 'Relics' calls this letter 'the classical instance' of the veneration of relics and says, after Thomas Aquinas, that relics are honored 'with a veneration which is not that of latria (divine worship)'; it also quotes Harnack, from the other side, that 'Most offensive ... was the worship of relics'. The site's cards set out each tradition's view with its sources: on honoring holy people at Acts 10, on the prayers of the saints at Revelation 5, and on relics at 2 Kings 13.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 9:24-25; Revelation 2:10; 1 Peter 3:18; John 20:28; Hebrews 13:7; Acts 10:25-26; Revelation 22:8-9

title: More precious than gems
sum: The centurion settled the quarrel by burning the body (18:1). Later the Christians gathered the bones, 'worth more than costly gems and more prized than gold', and laid them where it was fitting (18:2). There, the Lord willing, they would gather each year in joy to keep 'the birthday of his martyrdom', to remember those who had fought the contest and to prepare those still to come (18:3).

views.M: The church keeps the martyr's bones and plans to keep the day of his death each year as his 'birthday' (the notes at 18:2-3). The Catholic Encyclopedia's article 'Relics' calls this letter 'the classical instance' of the veneration of relics; the Orthodox Church in America keeps Polycarp's day on 23 February.
views.R: The centurion's burning was meant to leave nothing to honor; the Christians still gathered the bones. Eusebius's copy calls him by the Greek word for centurion, not the Latin loanword (variant).
views.N: The Bible records the burial of the faithful (Acts 8:2), Joseph's bones carried out of Egypt (Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19) and the dead man who touched Elisha's bones (2 Kings 13:21), but no church keeping a martyr's bones or his yearly day. The churches read these passages differently (the card at 2 Kings 13).

deep.b: The Catholic Encyclopedia quotes 18:2 for the early care of martyrs' remains and says 'special commemoration services of the martyrs ... were held on the anniversaries of their death' (Hassett, 'Martyr'). Its article 'Relics' (Thurston) quotes 18:2-3 as 'the classical instance' of the veneration of relics and says it 'is the keynote which is echoed in a multitude of similar passages found a little later in the patristic writers of both East and West'. The letter's own purpose for the feast is twofold: 'to remember those who have already fought the contest and to train and ready those still to come' (18:3). Whether relics should be venerated is the question of the site's card at 2 Kings 13; how to honor the saints, the cards at Acts 10 and Revelation 5.

title: The twelfth martyr
sum: Polycarp was the twelfth to die, with martyrs from Philadelphia, but he alone is remembered everywhere, even by the Gentiles, as a famous teacher and an outstanding martyr whose death followed the gospel (19:1). By his endurance he defeated the unjust ruler and now, with the apostles and all the righteous, glorifies God and blesses Jesus Christ, 'the Savior of our souls, the Pilot of our bodies, and the Shepherd of the catholic church throughout the world' (19:2).

views.H: Here Eusebius's quotation ends: Polycarp 'suffered martyrdom in Smyrna with the eleven from Philadelphia' (Church History 4.15.45). The Vienna manuscript (v) also ends with chapter 19 (Lake).
views.M: Polycarp's fame already outshines the others; the letter explains it by his life as well as his death.
views.N: 1 Peter 2:25 (Shepherd and Overseer of souls); Revelation 3:7-13 (Philadelphia).

title: Send the letter on
sum: Philomelium asked for a fuller account; this summary comes through 'our brother Marcion'. Send it on to the brothers farther away, so that they too may glorify the Lord (20:1). A doxology, greetings, and the name of the scribe, Evarestus, close the letter (20:2).

views.H: Lake: 'This is really the end of the book. What follows is a series of notes, which have been taken into the text.' The writer's name differs in the witnesses: Marcion, Marcus, Marcianus (variant).
views.R: Smyrna asks Philomelium to send the letter on (20:1), as Paul asked the Colossians to pass on theirs (Colossians 4:16).

title: The date
sum: A dating note: Polycarp was martyred on the second of Xanthicus, seven days before the Kalends of March, on a great Sabbath, at the eighth hour; arrested by Herod, when Philip of Tralles was high priest and Statius Quadratus proconsul, 'while Jesus Christ was reigning as King forever' (21:1).

views.H: The note gives the date in three calendars: the Macedonian month used at Smyrna, the Roman (23 February), and the Jewish 'great Sabbath'. Lake's introduction weighs Eusebius's 166-167, Waddington's 155, and Turner's and Schwartz's 156. The Catholic Encyclopedia favors 155 and allows that the note may have been altered later; Bart Ehrman holds that its officials do not fit one year.
views.R: The note names the provincial high priest and the proconsul. Lake: the closing phrase is 'pointedly inserted instead of a reference to the reigning Emperor'.

deep.b:
Lake's introduction: Eusebius's Chronicle dated the martyrdom 166-167, 'now ... almost universally abandoned', because the letter dates it to Saturday, Xanthicus 2, '23 February', under the proconsul Statius Quadratus, and Waddington (1864), from Aelius Aristides, 'showed that Quadratus became proconsul of Asia in 153-4. Now, Feb. 23 fell on a Saturday in 155.' The Catholic Encyclopedia gives Waddington's result as 'proconsul in 154-55 (the proconsul's year of office began in May)', which covers February 155; it tells how Schmid's case for 165-166 was undone by inscriptions (as Ramsay reported), concludes that Waddington's system, 'in spite of some very real difficulties', 'is in possession', and adds that 'the possibility of course remains that the subscription was tampered with by a later hand'. The 'great Sabbath' complicates the date: C. H. Turner argued for Purim, 22 February 156, and E. Schwartz for 'the Sabbath after the Passover' by Smyrna's Jewish reckoning, also 22 February 156 (Lake).

Bart Ehrman, citing T. D. Barnes (1967), turns the note against the letter: Philip was high priest 'in 149/50', but 'no conceivable argument will put the pro-consulate of Statius Quadratus before 153/4', so the note 'is written by someone living later' (his blog, 2023, from Forgery and Counterforgery, 2013).

title: The copyists
sum: A farewell asks that the readers walk by the gospel and be found in Polycarp's footsteps in Christ's kingdom (22:1). Then the copyists speak: Gaius copied the text from what Irenaeus, Polycarp's disciple, had; Socrates copied it in Corinth; and Pionius, guided by a revelation from Polycarp, found the worn copy and wrote it out again (22:2-3). The Moscow manuscript has a longer ending of its own.

views.H: The notes trace the text from Irenaeus to Pionius (Lake: 'supposed to have lived in the 4th century'). The Moscow manuscript's ending adds Irenaeus in Rome, the Marcion story and a voice heard in Rome (variant at 22:2). The Catholic Encyclopedia thinks the postscript came from the pseudo-Pionius who wrote a later Life of Polycarp.
views.M: The chain of copyists, each praying to be gathered with the chosen, shows how a martyr's story was kept and handed on by the church.
